title: Owe no one anything (Romans 13:8–14)
hookLine: except to love one another; love is the fulfilling of the law

lines: THE ONE DEBT YOU CAN'T PAY OFF.
cards: Plenty of friendships run on a quiet ledger. The friend who paid for lunch last time, so it's your turn. The neighbor who watched your dog, so you owe them one.
The twenty dollars your brother still hasn't paid back. Score gets kept, often without anyone meaning to, and it feels fair.

Paul has just been talking about paying what you owe: taxes to whom taxes are due, honor to whom honor is due. Settle up, he says. Then he names the one debt you can never pay off, and says to keep it.

teach.h: THE ONE DEBT THAT STAYS OPEN.
teach.b: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law." Clear every other debt; love stays open.

You never get to say: there, I've loved you enough, we're even. An old Christian writer, Origen, put it something like this: the debt of love remains with us always, and we pay it daily and always owe it.
Then Paul takes the commandments, don't commit adultery, don't kill, don't steal, don't covet, and says they're all summed up in one line from the law of Moses: love your neighbor as yourself.
"Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law."
Fulfilling in Greek is pleroma, fullness: love fills the law up to the brim. Jesus said much the same when he named the two great commandments. Then Paul looks at the clock.
The night is far spent, the day is at hand. Wake up. Cast off the works of darkness, and put on the armor of light.
He ends with a line with a well-known afterlife: "But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof."
Centuries later, a restless teacher named Augustine sat weeping in a garden in Milan.
He heard a child's voice nearby, singing, take up and read.

teach.h: LOVE IS THE FULFILLING OF THE LAW.
teach.b: He opened Paul's letters, and his eyes fell on these very lines. A light of peace, he wrote, flooded his heart. He tells the story himself, in his Confessions.

how: Romans 13:11–14 is a traditional reading for the first Sunday of Advent in some churches, and Christians tell Augustine's conversion story as an example of how a single verse can change a life.

o: a law kept exactly, letter by letter
a debt paid off completely, all at once
fullness: filled all the way to the brim

games.q: what's inside the passage — tap the pairs.

s: Paul says to keep every debt paid, including love
love is the one debt that stays open: "owe no man any thing, but to love one another."
in a garden in Milan he heard take up and read, and his eyes fell on these lines.
Paul says love replaces the law and throws it away
love is the fulfilling of the law: it fills it to the brim.

games.q: you're Augustine, weeping in a garden in Milan. a child's voice sings: take up and read. Paul's letters lie nearby. what do you do?
o: ignore it: just a children's game.
pick up the book and read the first lines you see.
go inside and ask a priest what it means.
games.why: he opened Paul's letters to Romans 13: "put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." he later wrote that a light of peace flooded his heart.

practice: Scan your life for something you owe, a borrowed book, five dollars, a thank-you note, a reply you've put off, a call to someone who always calls you first, and pick the smallest real one and decide when you'll pay it.
Then picture someone you love and notice how much you still owe them in love, and owe it gladly. If you pray, you can give thanks for that debt.

wordCard.voice: Pleroma. The Greek word for fullness: love fills the law up to the brim, the one debt that never closes.

orig.note: Greek: fullness, fulfilling. love fills the law up to the brim.

carryVoice: Your line: love fulfils the law. It's the one debt worth keeping open. Day three hundred twenty-eight, done.
